How to Address People in Japanese: Names and Titles

Kanjidon Team · Jan 31, 2026

Japanese address choices depend on relationship, setting, role and the preferences of the people involved. Pronouns are often omitted when context identifies the person, but no single form works in every situation or disappears from every conversation. Observe how a group addresses one another and ask when the stakes are high.

Omission Is Common, Not Mandatory

Japanese often leaves out a subject or addressee that both speakers can recover. コーヒー、飲みますか can ask whether someone wants coffee without saying “you.” When identification matters, a name, role, kinship term or pronoun may be appropriate.

Names and Common Suffixes

FormCommon roleImportant limit
name + さんPolite or respectful address in many neutral adult contextsWorkplaces, professions and personal preferences may use a title or another form
name + 様Formal correspondence, service language and elevated respectToo formal for many ordinary peer interactions
name + ちゃんAffectionate or familiar address, often for children, pets or close relationshipsDo not assume familiarity or impose it on someone
name + 君Familiar or hierarchical address in some schools and workplacesNot simply “for boys”; usage varies by institution, generation and relationship
name + 先生Address for teachers and some recognized professionalsUse depends on the role and convention, not a generic label for every expert

How to Address a Doctor

A doctor may be addressed as 先生 or surname + 先生, such as 田中先生. お医者さん is a respectful everyday way to refer to a doctor; combining お医者 with 先生 is not the standard title. In a clinic, follow how staff introduce the person.

あなた Depends on Context

あなた can be neutral in questionnaires, general statements, translations or situations where the addressee is not named. In direct conversation it may sound distant, pointed or unnecessary when a name or omitted subject would fit better. Tone and relationship matter, so “あなた is rude” and “あなた is the normal English you” are both incomplete rules.

First Name, Family Name or Role

  • Use the form in the person’s introduction, signature or name badge when available.
  • Family name + さん is a reasonable starting hypothesis in many adult encounters, not a universal command.
  • Schools, international teams and close groups may prefer given names.
  • Titles such as 部長 or 先生 can be used alone or with a name according to local practice.
  • Do not switch to a bare given name because a textbook labels the relationship “friend”; listen for mutual usage.

First-Person Forms Also Carry Register

FormBroad tendencyWhy context matters
私（わたし／わたくし）Widely usable; わたくし is more formalCasual gendered impressions vary by speaker and setting
僕（ぼく）Often masculine and relatively softAlso used by some speakers outside that stereotype
俺（おれ）Strongly informal and often masculineCan sound close, rough or inappropriate depending on the group
あたしCasual and often feminineNot a formal default
自分（じぶん）Reflexive or self-reference in some regions and groupsIts referent can depend heavily on context

A Practical Decision Sequence

  • Can the addressee be omitted naturally?
  • Did the person or host provide a preferred form?
  • Is a professional or organizational title expected here?
  • Does name + さん fit the observed level of formality?
  • If uncertain, can you ask or mirror a respectful introduction?

Official and Teaching Sources

  • Agency for Cultural Affairs: Guidelines for Honorific Language
  • Japan Foundation Marugoto teacher notes on names and honorific suffixes
